Zuma at the Zondo Commission

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
This week, former president Jacob Zuma takes the stand at the Zondo Commission on state capture, the latest attempt to have him answer a litany of corruption allegations.

Unique Selling Point:
The week of 15th to 19th of July 2019 is scheduled to be the first time Former President Jacob Zuma will appear in front of the Zondo Commission, to answer to the many accusations concerning his alleged pivotal role in state capture. Speculation is already rife on whether or not he will fully co-operate, but in any case, it is one of the most anticipated events in South African democratic history.

Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo’s judicial commission of inquiry has been tasked to investigate widespread allegations of state capture. Their challenge is to piece together the ‘true extent of state capture and how certain individuals and businesses’ benefited from the state financially.
Will the pointing fingers aimed at Zuma, so far during the inquiry, amount to anything more than a TRC-like release from guilt by the perpetrators of wrong-doings... without any repercussions? Will we actually hear the full low-down from Zuma? Or will we have to just wait for him to write his book?

With the collaboration of political analysts, we will provide the context to this historic week. The Commission, with its team of evidence leaders... The accusers of Zuma... The appearance of Zuma with the support of his legal team and rallying citizens...
Former president Jacob Zuma, himself, will most likely determine the core narrative of his week at the Zondo Commission.

Summary:
Under the watch of President Zuma, the tentacles of state capture spread throughout the South African state apparatus and aligned businesses. His particular methods of supervision of the state led to the promotion of now distrusted personnel and ministers, those with more loyalty to private entities that could fill their pockets, than to the ethos of public service.

After his presidency, Zuma still surrounds himself with characters tarnished by the reputation of greed. The head of his legal team for the hearings is Daniel Mantsha. The name of Mantsha was discredited in his time as chairperson of Denel, mainly because of the Denel Asia project‚ a joint venture between Denel and Gupta-owned companies. Furthermore, Mantsha has in the past been struck of the roll.

At the end of the week, beyond sub-standard supervision of the state, what can Zuma be held accountable for at the Zondo Commission? After all, he has repeatedly pleaded his innocence of direct involvement in state capture machinations. Furthermore, he has resisted compliance with any investigative body that he deems not to be an independent platform. Already, he refused to answer direct questions from public protector Thuli Madonsela concerning his relationship with his son Duduzane and to the Gupta family – both parties deeply entrenched in the South African state capture saga.

If Zuma co-operates with the leaders of evidence, we will cover his version of events, and weigh them up against the allegations. If he decides to work against the system then we will represent him with the empty chair scenario... in his place at the commission, an empty chair... and discuss the witness’s allegations further. Interviews with the likes of political analyst Professor William Gumede and commentator Songezo Zibi, will endeavour to pinpoint the impact of Zuma’s testimony within the broad remit of the commission.

Further information:
The three pillars of state: parliament, the executive and the judiciary have, Zuma argues, not been fully 'captured' by private entities for their own gain. However, evidence shows that people high up in each pillar have been captured by private entities for their own gain... enough people to constitute a crisis of government. Former President Jacob Zuma’s denial of state capture itself rests on semantics. He prefers the former definition of state capture to the latter and hence argues that the South African state was not captured.

Zuma has repeatedly denied any complicity in the corrupt dealings encompassing state capture. However, the Zondo Commission wants his side of the story. Not least, because many witnesses who have appeared before the commission have made allegations about Zuma’s role in state capture and corruption. No cast iron evidence has materialized confirming Zuma’s alleged wrong-doings, so will he take the chance to put the record straight from his point of view or will he refuse to directly answer the accusations made against him? In either case, we will highlight the major incidents of state capture and corruption where witnesses have testified that Zuma has played a major role.

Main players in the Zondo Commission:
The Zondo Commission is currently gathering evidence and is expected to deliver its report to the President possibly in 2020.
Chairperson of the Commission:
Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo
Evidence Leaders (comprised of the legal team for the commission):
Advocate Paul Joseph Pretorius (Head of Legal Team), Isaac Maleka, Leah Gcabashe, Thandi Norman

We will isolate testimonies by those that have already appeared in front of the commission where they implicate Zuma in state capture. For instance:
- Bosasa former COO Angelo Agrizzi alleged, in front of the commission, that bribes were delivered regularly to Jacob Zuma, at the behest of Bosasa CEO Gavin Watson.
- Former GCIS CEO Themba Maseka surmised at the commission that “because the GCIS entity was operating within the presidency, and [the Guptas] felt they had influence, rather than control, over the president, it would be easy for [the Guptas] to access the resources that were located in GCIS”... “we need cash, what is the quickest way to get cash, let’s get to the entities that report to the person we have influence over”
- Former finance minister Nhlanhla Nene testified that Zuma pressurized him over the Russian nuclear deal.


What does Zuma have to say in response?
We will find out during the week.

What are Zuma’s team tactics?
Zuma denies he has been or ever was ‘captured’ and disputes the notion of state capture itself. The political analysts can elaborate.

Expert:
Mr. Songezo Zibi
Prof. William Gumede

Press Release:


Former President Zuma Testifies
It’s been a week of legal head-butting and obfuscation in the much-anticipated appearance of former President Jacob Zuma before the Judicial Commission into allegations of state capture led by Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo. Claiming he’s the target of a long-standing political conspiracy, the former president raised fresh allegations of a plot to kill him and denied his friendship with the Gupta family had any bearing on government appointments. Carte Blanche examines the importance of this week’s testimony in the bigger political and judicial landscape.
Producer: Sophia Phirippides
Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


LINK: There’s a massive police presence and an air of anticipation as we await the arrival of the former president along with a throng of foreign and local journalists. It is Jacob Zuma’s turn to testify before the Zondo commission,

SOUND UP: TAKING THE OATH…I, JACOB GEDLEYIHLEKISA ZUMA…//

VO: BUT how much of his truth WOULD he be willing to share...

SOUND UP: DO SOLEMNLY SWEAR TO TELL THE TRUTH…

VO: Nobody quite knew what to expect when Zuma took the stand in Parktown, Johannesburg, on Monday.The chairperson of the commission, Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo, playing by the book, to keep Zuma in the chair as long as possible,//

// Head evidence leader for the Commission, Advocate Paul Joseph Pretorius, and his team//
Facing off their counterparts, Zuma’s legal counsel headed by Advocate Daniel Mantsha and Advocate Muzi Sikhakhane. And then the gloves were off, Zuma’s apparent legal tactic, to object and cry foul.!!!

Sikhakhane: Now that he has started on his condescension, let me deal with it, now!

VO: But first, the 77-year-old former President SEEMED TO TAKE control of the narrative, outlining conspiracies and plots, starting in the early nineties.

SOUND UP: ZUMA - There were three intelligence organisatons that had a plan to begin in 1990 a process of character assassination of Zuma.

VO: Things had become more sinister, ACCORDING TO ZUMA..

SOUND UP: ZUMA - Before I die, I tell the story. The plan to kill me in Durban was detailed. It involved people brought from outside the country. (suicidal bombers were supposed to do to me)

LINK: Jacob Zuma set the tone for his testimony here at the commission saying there was a conspiracy against him, that he’d been vilified and that he’d been painted as the king of corruption.

VO: Although he didn’t name President Ramaphosa, Zuma’s inferences were clear when he spoke about his OWN resignation as president last year.

Sound Up Zuma: We'll meet somewhere

ZUMA: Those people in my organisation who wanted to take Zuma out as intelligence head, ….//they create a situation as I am about to go for the State of the Nation Address, Zuma must not give this one he must resign.

VO: Outside the commission Zuma acolytes were bussed in for the day, as his allies rallied for support, in what they deemed to be an unfair commission.

Sound Up crowd
VO: But Zuma wasn't going to get into the hot seat without some tactical manoeuvring of his own. He began by naming former ANC comrades as ALLEGED spies, SOME OF THEM ONCE MINISTERS IN HIS CABINET, like Nwako RamatlHodi, AND SIPHIWE NYANDA, FORMER MINISTER OF COMMUNICATION.
VO: RamAtlhodi alleged in 2017 that Eskom Chair Ben Ngubane and chief executive Brian Molefe HAD requested that he terminate Glencore's mining licenses, IN ORDER TO facilitate the sale of its Optimum Coal mine to Gupta owned company, Tegeta.
MR NGOAKO RAMATLHODI: It ended with me saying I am not able to just revoke the licenses like that,
VO: Both Nyanda and Ramathlhodi have denied these allegations and Ramatlhodi has challenged the former president to undergo a lie detector test. But, what was clear from day one of his testimony was that Zuma would expose ANC fault lines, rather than take responsibility, or spill the beans on corruption, a view echoed by Professor William Gumede, founder of Democracy Works Foundation.
Gumede: Their strategy which is, you know, which is personified by the strategy of Jacob Zuma is to, to fight back by almost trying to show that they are being politically prosecuted by Ramaphosa and his faction and secondly trying to say that no they've done all the bad things that happen was done by external players: foreign spies, apartheid spies, and so on.

LINK: Some supporters of Jacob Zuma are asking why he has become the poster child for state capture

VO: Former newspaper editor and author, Songezo Zibi says corruption is also rife in the private sector, but the state belongs to all of us .

Derek: Ace Magashule come out and said that all companies dealing with this state should be investigated not just Gupta's?

Songezo: Public sector corruption is nothing we don’t without accomplices in the private sector. Everybody who was an accomplice must go in and say at the commission as a principle. That's correct

Zuma: why the report must say we are investigating capture…

Derek: he denies that the state has been captured.

Songezo: large portions of the state were captured for corrupt intent by various people wanted to harm this country and accumulate wealth for themselves.

VO: But the former president continued to deny that his relationship with the Guptas was suspect in any way


Zuma: I've never did anything with them, unlawfully or whatever, they just remained friends, and I've wondered why I'm accused,

Beat// Day 2
VO: On Tuesday came another Zuma ‘bombshell’. More death threats, - a phone call to his personal assistant.

ZUMA: this person said 'you must tell Zuma that we are going to kill him, and we are also going to kill his children

VO: But the Former President, has not been the only one to receive death threats, whistle blowers and detractors during the Zuma years were also fearing for their lives.

Songezo: I have had conversations with people who did not want me or them to have their cell phones. And as we are walking there we are whispering because they are frightened.

VO: Dr Masimba Dahwa who was chief procurement officer at South African Airways (SAA) and testified in June last year, dared to butt heads with chairperson Dudu Miyeni, a known Zuma ally and confidante.

DR MASIMBA PHILLIP DAHWA: the key message for me to South African Airways was please do not proceed with this practice as it is unlawful.

VO: He paid the price, and feared for his life.

Songezo: I was nearly in tears when he said his house is going to be repossessed by the bank. he's not able to take his kids to school and his only crime was he said no. What was most tragic for me is that it was usually those kinds of people that were not wanted because it was their sense of public service that made them say no.

VO: Zuma's presence by day two of his testimony, was by no means enlightening. He denied every allegation that came his way.

SOUND UP: ZUMA – put a few of his denial bites back to back

Beat// Day 3
VO: By Wednesday, the former President complained of victimisation and the ‘line of questioning’. This was after Evidence leader Advocate Paul Pretorius broached the testimony of former minister of Public Enterprises Barbara Hogan in November last year, on the appointment of Siyabonga Gama as Transnet CEO.
MS BARBARA HOGAN: Chair, I was extremely shocked. The President would not hear of any candidate except Siyabonga Gama.
VO: Evidence Leader Adv Paul Pretorius questioned the former president on whether he was aware that there was a case of misconduct against Mr gama, and that the board did not want to recommend him.
Pretorius: Were you aware of those sentiments
Zuma: Yes
VO: After further questioning around the ANC's deployment policies, Zuma's's legal council Advocate Muzi Sikhakhane objected to his client being subjected to what he said was tantamount to cross examination.

Songezo: We work with public assets with public money. The ethical standing in the integrity of that person is critical. The experience of that person is critical. So what happened was that the transformation imperative was abused to create an excuse for inappropriate appointments in the public service whose desire was to harm the country.

LINK: More drama at the commission on Wednesday after the lunch break. JACOB ZUMA’S legal representative saying that his client was brought to the commission under false pretences and he now needs to make up his mind on whether he wants to be here or not. They've adjourned to make that decision.

Gumede: If Jacob Zuma is seen by the public to be treated with kid gloves by different rules then the authority and credibility of the commission drops and declines.

VO: And the drama continued on Friday when Judge Zondo announced that the former president was withdrawing. But with one more try behind closed doors, they emerged…

Derek Zuma interaction…
Zuma: I'll be back..

VO: it appears that at least in theory Jacob Zuma will be returning to face the commission.

Sound Up Zuma: We'll meet somewhere ZUMA: Those people in my organisation who wanted to take Zuma out as intelligence head, ….//they create a situation as I am about to go for the State of the Nation Address, Zuma must not give this one he must resign. VO: Outside the commission Zuma acolytes were bussed in for the day, as his allies rallied for support, in what they deemed to be an unfair commission. Sound Up crowd VO: But Zuma wasn't going to get into the hot seat without some tactical manoeuvring of his own. He began by naming former ANC comrades as ALLEGED spies, SOME OF THEM ONCE MINISTERS IN HIS CABINET, like Nwako RamatlHodi, AND SIPHIWE NYANDA, FORMER MINISTER OF COMMUNICATION. VO: RamAtlhodi alleged in 2017 that Eskom Chair Ben Ngubane and chief executive Brian Molefe HAD requested that he terminate Glencore's mining licenses, IN ORDER TO facilitate the sale of its Optimum Coal mine to Gupta owned company, Tegeta. MR NGOAKO RAMATLHODI: It ended with me saying I am not able to just revoke the licenses like that, VO: Both Nyanda and Ramathlhodi have denied these allegations and Ramatlhodi has challenged the former president to undergo a lie detector test. But, what was clear from day one of his testimony was that Zuma would expose ANC fault lines, rather than take responsibility, or spill the beans on corruption, a view echoed by Professor William Gumede, founder of Democracy Works Foundation. Gumede: Their strategy which is, you know, which is personified by the strategy of Jacob Zuma is to, to fight back by almost trying to show that they are being politically prosecuted by Ramaphosa and his faction and secondly trying to say that no they've done all the bad things that happen was done by external players: foreign spies, apartheid spies, and so on. LINK: Some supporters of Jacob Zuma are asking why he has become the poster child for state capture VO: Former newspaper editor and author, Songezo Zibi says corruption is also rife in the private sector, but the state belongs to all of us . Derek: Ace Magashule come out and said that all companies dealing with this state should be investigated not just Gupta's? Songezo: Public sector corruption is nothing we don’t without accomplices in the private sector. Everybody who was an accomplice must go in and say at the commission as a principle. That's correct Zuma: why the report must say we are investigating capture… Derek: he denies that the state has been captured. Songezo: large portions of the state were captured for corrupt intent by various people wanted to harm this country and accumulate wealth for themselves. VO: But the former president continued to deny that his relationship with the Guptas was suspect in any way Zuma: I've never did anything with them, unlawfully or whatever, they just remained friends, and I've wondered why I'm accused, Beat// Day 2 VO: On Tuesday came another Zuma ‘bombshell’. More death threats, - a phone call to his personal assistant. ZUMA: this person said 'you must tell Zuma that we are going to kill him, and we are also going to kill his children VO: But the Former President, has not been the only one to receive death threats, whistle blowers and detractors during the Zuma years were also fearing for their lives. Songezo: I have had conversations with people who did not want me or them to have their cell phones. And as we are walking there we are whispering because they are frightened. VO: Dr Masimba Dahwa who was chief procurement officer at South African Airways (SAA) and testified in June last year, dared to butt heads with chairperson Dudu Miyeni, a known Zuma ally and confidante. DR MASIMBA PHILLIP DAHWA: the key message for me to South African Airways was please do not proceed with this practice as it is unlawful. VO: He paid the price, and feared for his life. Songezo: I was nearly in tears when he said his house is going to be repossessed by the bank. he's not able to take his kids to school and his only crime was he said no. What was most tragic for me is that it was usually those kinds of people that were not wanted because it was their sense of public service that made them say no. VO: Zuma's presence by day two of his testimony, was by no means enlightening. He denied every allegation that came his way. SOUND UP: ZUMA – put a few of his denial bites back to back Beat// Day 3 VO: By Wednesday, the former President complained of victimisation and the ‘line of questioning’. This was after Evidence leader Advocate Paul Pretorius broached the testimony of former minister of Public Enterprises Barbara Hogan in November last year, on the appointment of Siyabonga Gama as Transnet CEO. MS BARBARA HOGAN: Chair, I was extremely shocked. The President would not hear of any candidate except Siyabonga Gama. VO: Evidence Leader Adv Paul Pretorius questioned the former president on whether he was aware that there was a case of misconduct against Mr gama, and that the board did not want to recommend him. Pretorius: Were you aware of those sentiments Zuma: Yes VO: After further questioning around the ANC's deployment policies, Zuma's's legal council Advocate Muzi Sikhakhane objected to his client being subjected to what he said was tantamount to cross examination. Songezo: We work with public assets with public money. The ethical standing in the integrity of that person is critical. The experience of that person is critical. So what happened was that the transformation imperative was abused to create an excuse for inappropriate appointments in the public service whose desire was to harm the country. LINK: More drama at the commission on Wednesday after the lunch break. JACOB ZUMA’S legal representative saying that his client was brought to the commission under false pretences and he now needs to make up his mind on whether he wants to be here or not. They've adjourned to make that decision. Gumede: If Jacob Zuma is seen by the public to be treated with kid gloves by different rules then the authority and credibility of the commission drops and declines. VO: And the drama continued on Friday when Judge Zondo announced that the former president was withdrawing. But with one more try behind closed doors, they emerged… Derek Zuma interaction… Zuma: I'll be back.. VO: it appears that at least in theory Jacob Zuma will be returning to face the commission.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): This week, former president Jacob Zuma takes the stand at the Zondo Commission on state capture, the latest attempt to have him answer a litany of corruption allegations.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The week of 15th to 19th of July 2019 is scheduled to be the first time Former President Jacob Zuma will appear in front of the Zondo Commission, to answer to the many accusations concerning his alleged pivotal role in state capture. Speculation is already rife on whether or not he will fully co-operate, but in any case, it is one of the most anticipated events in South African democratic history. Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo’s judicial commission of inquiry has been tasked to investigate widespread allegations of state capture. Their challenge is to piece together the ‘true extent of state capture and how certain individuals and businesses’ benefited from the state financially. Will the pointing fingers aimed at Zuma, so far during the inquiry, amount to anything more than a TRC-like release from guilt by the perpetrators of wrong-doings... without any repercussions? Will we actually hear the full low-down from Zuma? Or will we have to just wait for him to write his book? With the collaboration of political analysts, we will provide the context to this historic week. The Commission, with its team of evidence leaders... The accusers of Zuma... The appearance of Zuma with the support of his legal team and rallying citizens... Former president Jacob Zuma, himself, will most likely determine the core narrative of his week at the Zondo Commission.
metadata.Summary: Under the watch of President Zuma, the tentacles of state capture spread throughout the South African state apparatus and aligned businesses. His particular methods of supervision of the state led to the promotion of now distrusted personnel and ministers, those with more loyalty to private entities that could fill their pockets, than to the ethos of public service. After his presidency, Zuma still surrounds himself with characters tarnished by the reputation of greed. The head of his legal team for the hearings is Daniel Mantsha. The name of Mantsha was discredited in his time as chairperson of Denel, mainly because of the Denel Asia project‚ a joint venture between Denel and Gupta-owned companies. Furthermore, Mantsha has in the past been struck of the roll. At the end of the week, beyond sub-standard supervision of the state, what can Zuma be held accountable for at the Zondo Commission? After all, he has repeatedly pleaded his innocence of direct involvement in state capture machinations. Furthermore, he has resisted compliance with any investigative body that he deems not to be an independent platform. Already, he refused to answer direct questions from public protector Thuli Madonsela concerning his relationship with his son Duduzane and to the Gupta family – both parties deeply entrenched in the South African state capture saga. If Zuma co-operates with the leaders of evidence, we will cover his version of events, and weigh them up against the allegations. If he decides to work against the system then we will represent him with the empty chair scenario... in his place at the commission, an empty chair... and discuss the witness’s allegations further. Interviews with the likes of political analyst Professor William Gumede and commentator Songezo Zibi, will endeavour to pinpoint the impact of Zuma’s testimony within the broad remit of the commission.
metadata.Further information: The three pillars of state: parliament, the executive and the judiciary have, Zuma argues, not been fully 'captured' by private entities for their own gain. However, evidence shows that people high up in each pillar have been captured by private entities for their own gain... enough people to constitute a crisis of government. Former President Jacob Zuma’s denial of state capture itself rests on semantics. He prefers the former definition of state capture to the latter and hence argues that the South African state was not captured. Zuma has repeatedly denied any complicity in the corrupt dealings encompassing state capture. However, the Zondo Commission wants his side of the story. Not least, because many witnesses who have appeared before the commission have made allegations about Zuma’s role in state capture and corruption. No cast iron evidence has materialized confirming Zuma’s alleged wrong-doings, so will he take the chance to put the record straight from his point of view or will he refuse to directly answer the accusations made against him? In either case, we will highlight the major incidents of state capture and corruption where witnesses have testified that Zuma has played a major role. Main players in the Zondo Commission: The Zondo Commission is currently gathering evidence and is expected to deliver its report to the President possibly in 2020. Chairperson of the Commission: Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo Evidence Leaders (comprised of the legal team for the commission): Advocate Paul Joseph Pretorius (Head of Legal Team), Isaac Maleka, Leah Gcabashe, Thandi Norman We will isolate testimonies by those that have already appeared in front of the commission where they implicate Zuma in state capture. For instance: - Bosasa former COO Angelo Agrizzi alleged, in front of the commission, that bribes were delivered regularly to Jacob Zuma, at the behest of Bosasa CEO Gavin Watson. - Former GCIS CEO Themba Maseka surmised at the commission that “because the GCIS entity was operating within the presidency, and [the Guptas] felt they had influence, rather than control, over the president, it would be easy for [the Guptas] to access the resources that were located in GCIS”... “we need cash, what is the quickest way to get cash, let’s get to the entities that report to the person we have influence over” - Former finance minister Nhlanhla Nene testified that Zuma pressurized him over the Russian nuclear deal. What does Zuma have to say in response? We will find out during the week. What are Zuma’s team tactics? Zuma denies he has been or ever was ‘captured’ and disputes the notion of state capture itself. The political analysts can elaborate.
